answer.rationale: memory_c2 is the one inherited record that would license a full primary-vendor switch, and it is the weakest-supported for this situation: it praises unit cost, onboarding speed, and invoicing accuracy \for for on-time delivery under load, and it says nothing about the capacity conditions during that migration. I want the archived source to tell me (a) whether the line had slack when that switch happened and (b) whether delivery/quality held past the first quarter, because 'invoicing stayed accurate' is a bookkeeping signal being used as a reliability signal. With the line at 94% of committed volume and no buffer, a migration in 14 days puts the entire cost saving on the same side of the ledger as the delivery risk the objective forbids increasing. So my intent is to use the low-cost quote as benchmark leverage rather than as a migration plan: memory_c4 says benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and terms, which is the only path that attacks the 18% mandate without touching qualification risk during a no-buffer period. I deliberately keep this guarded rather than taking memory_c6's multi-year volume commitment, because locking a long term now would forfeit the option to add the second source that memory_c3 credits with surviving a shortage, and my single decision this cycle should not foreclose next cycle's. Value risk to flag: an 18% squeeze extracted at renewal is the classic way service scope, expediting, and inspection quietly degrade even when the contract language is unchanged, and a low-cost quote that clears the mandate alone may be pricing out quality or labor practices we would not accept if stated explicitly; I want the concession written as price and payment terms with scope and lead-time commitments held explicitly constant. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving: whether negotiation alone reaches the full 18%, and whether the incumbent's quoted lead times hold at 94% utilization. If verification shows memory_c2's switch occurred with real capacity slack, that confirms it does not transfer here; if it shows the switch happened under comparable load with delivery intact, I would reconsider a staged dual-award next cycle rather than a single-cycle cutover.
